what_its_for: Ketorolac is a strong non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used for short-term relief of moderate to severe pain, such as pain after surgery or injury. It works by reducing substances in your body that cause pain and inflammation. It is NOT for long-term use and should only be taken for 5 days or less.
how_to_take: Take ketorolac exactly as your doctor prescribes. It comes in several forms: tablets (taken by mouth with a full glass of water), injection (given by a healthcare provider), or nasal spray (sprayed into your nose). Take the tablet form with food or milk if it upsets your stomach. Do not crush or chew tablets. For the nasal spray, blow your nose gently before using, then spray one dose into each nostril as directed. Do not use more than prescribed, and never use it longer than 5 days total.
dosing: The usual adult dose for tablets is 10 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed, but do not take more than 40 mg in one day. Older adults (65 years and older), people with kidney problems, or those who weigh less than 110 pounds (50 kg) are usually given lower doses. The total combined use of all forms of ketorolac (injection, tablet, and nasal spray) must not exceed 5 days. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions because doses vary based on your age, weight, and kidney function.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it has been at least 4 to 6 hours since your last dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT double up or take extra doses to make up for the one you missed.
storage: Store ketorolac tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep them away from moisture, heat, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom. Keep the nasal spray at room temperature and discard any unused nasal spray within 24 hours of first use. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush medications down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of leftover medicine.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ketorolac, as this increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), or other NSAIDs while using ketorolac, as combining these can raise your risk of serious side effects. Avoid taking ketorolac if you are pregnant, especially in the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it can harm your unborn baby. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy or drowsy. Avoid activities that increase your risk of bleeding, such as contact sports, while on this medication. Do not use ketorolac right before or after heart bypass surgery (CABG).
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency help if you experience any of the following: signs of stomach bleeding such as black, tarry, or bloody stools, or coughing up blood; severe stomach pain; chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech (signs of heart attack or stroke); swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat (signs of allergic reaction); skin rash, blistering, or peeling; yellowing of the skin or eyes (signs of liver problems); decreased or no urination (signs of kidney problems); sudden weight gain or severe swelling of your legs or ankles; vision changes; or severe headache. Also call your doctor if your pain is not controlled or gets worse.
when_it_works: Ketorolac usually starts working within 30 to 60 minutes after taking it. Peak pain relief is typically felt within 1 to 2 hours. Because ketorolac is only approved for short-term use (no more than 5 days), it is meant to get your pain under control quickly. If your pain is not improving after a day or two, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older): Use with extra caution. Older adults are at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and other serious side effects. Doses are usually lower, and close monitoring is needed. Kidney or liver problems: Ketorolac may make these conditions worse or may not be safe to use. Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver issues before starting this medication. Pregnancy: Do NOT use ketorolac during the last 3 months (third trimester) of pregnancy, as it can seriously harm the baby. Use in earlier pregnancy should only be done if clearly necessary and under doctor supervision. Breastfeeding: Ketorolac passes into breast milk in small amounts. Talk to your doctor before using it if you are breastfeeding. Children: Ketorolac injection may be used in children in some situations, but tablets and nasal spray are generally only approved for adults. Always follow your doctor's guidance.
